solution:
Section 16.1.2 of this chapter states outright that oxidative rancidity "is caused by free radical reaction initiated by light (photo oxidation) or catalysed by either enzymes or metal ions". The reaction is therefore a **free radical** reaction.

Why the others fail. It is not an *addition* reaction: nothing adds across the \(\mathrm{C=C}\) bonds of the unsaturated fat — the chapter says the unsaturated fat molecules **break down** during the oxidation to give volatile aldehydes and carboxylic acids. It is not a *substitution* reaction: no atom or group on the fat is replaced by another. It is not a *combination* reaction either: two reactants do not unite into a single product, since the products named are a mixture of shorter aldehydes and acids. Only the free-radical description matches what the chapter says happens.

Section 16.3.1 (a) defines soaps as "sodium or potassium salts of long chain fatty acids" which "are obtained by **alkaline hydrolysis** of natural oils and fats with NaOH or KOH. This is called saponification reaction." Saponification is therefore carried out by alkaline hydrolysis.

Why the others fail. *Oxidation* is the process behind oxidative rancidity of fats (§16.1.2), not their conversion to soap, and no oxidising agent appears in the saponification equation. *Polymerisation* joins monomers into a large molecule, whereas saponification does the opposite — it cleaves a triester into three fatty-acid salt molecules plus glycerol. *Free radical formation* is again the rancidity mechanism; saponification is an ionic reaction of hydroxide ion with an ester.

Section 16.2.1 states that the active ingredient of willow bark, salicylic acid, is 2-hydroxybenzoic acid, and that "the compound aspirin which is **acetyl derivative of salicylic acid** was found to have fewer side effects than salicylic acid." The acetyl derivative of salicylic acid is acetyl salicylic acid, so that is aspirin's chemical name.

Why the others fail. *Salicylic acid* is the parent compound aspirin is made from, not aspirin itself — the chapter contrasts the two, noting aspirin has fewer side effects. *Chloroxylenol* is a chlorinated phenol used as an antiseptic (the active ingredient of dettol, §16.2.2 a) and is not an analgesic. *Thymol* is the non-toxic antiseptic obtained from oil of thyme, again from §16.2.2 a.

Three of the four are antiseptics drawn from §16.2.2 (a): trichlorophenol (TCP) and chloroxylenol are named there as "two of the most common phenol derivatives in use" as antiseptics, and dettol is the popular antiseptic whose active ingredient is chloroxylenol. Paracetamol belongs to a different section entirely — §16.2.1 introduces it as "a less problematic pain-killer", that is an analgesic/antipyretic. It is therefore the odd one out.

Why the others fail as the odd one out. Dettol, chloroxylenol and trichlorophenol all share two properties paracetamol does not: each is an antiseptic, and each is or contains a chlorinated phenol. Any one of them removed still leaves a set of chlorophenolic antiseptics, so none of them breaks the pattern; only paracetamol does, on both counts.

Section 16.2.2 (b) records that Paul Ehrlich "investigated arsenic based organic compounds" and "discovered the first effective treatment of syphilis, the synthetic antibiotic named **salvarsan**". Salvarsan is thus the arsenic-based antibiotic.

Why the others fail. An *azodye* is a dye, not an antibiotic — the chapter mentions it only because Ehrlich noticed a structural similarity between salvarsan and azodyes, which led him onward. *Prontosil* is the diazo antibacterial he synthesised afterwards, in 1932; it contains nitrogen and sulphur, not arsenic. *Sulphapyridine* is described as one of the most effective of the sulpha drugs analogous to sulphanilamide, and again contains no arsenic.

Browning of cut fruit is the oxidation of released polyphenols to quinones. Section 16.1.2 (i) states that "this browning reaction can be slowed down using reducing agents such as \(\mathrm{SO_2}\), ascorbic acid (vitamin C) or by change of pH by adding edible acid such as lemon juice (citric acid) or vinegar." Of the four choices only \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) appears there, and it works because it is a reducing agent — it opposes the oxidation.

Why the others fail. \(\mathrm{SO_3}\) is the higher oxide of sulphur and is not a reducing agent; it is also not named anywhere in this chapter. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) does lower the pH but is a strong mineral acid, not one of the *edible* acids the chapter allows, and it is not listed. \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) is washing soda, mentioned in §16.3.1 (a) for softening hard water; being a base it would raise the pH rather than lower it, which is the wrong direction for slowing the browning.

Section 16.1.2 (ii) states that "rancidity of milk and butter is due to the release of four, six and eight carbon fatty acids (butanoic, hexanoic and octanoic acids) on hydrolysis." The four-carbon acid, butanoic acid, is commonly called butyric acid and is the one associated with the rancid flavour of fats.

Why the others fail. *Glycerol* is the other hydrolysis product of a fat; it is a sweet-tasting triol and is not responsible for the rancid smell — the chapter attributes rancidity to the fatty-acid half, not the glycerol half. *Protein* is a separate class of nutrient (§16.1) and takes no part in the hydrolysis or oxidation of fats. *Saturated fat* is the intact triglyceride; it is the substance that turns rancid, not the chemical that causes the rancid flavour, and the chapter is explicit that the flavour comes from the free acids (and, for oxidative rancidity, from volatile aldehydes and carboxylic acids) that are released.

Section 16.1.2 (iii) states that "there is some evidence that eating large amounts of saturated or trans unsaturated fats, increase the tendency of cholesterol getting deposited in blood vessels. **Cis fats do not cause formation of such deposits and decrease chance of developing coronary heart disease.**" Mono unsaturated fats are cis unsaturated fats — the chapter notes the cis isomer is the most common form of unsaturated fats — so they are the ones that carry a health benefit.

Why the others fail. *Saturated fats* are named in the sentence above as increasing cholesterol deposition, so they are harmful rather than beneficial. *Trans fats* are named in the same sentence, and the chapter adds that they "are difficult to metabolize and may build up to dangerous levels in fatty tissue". Since two of the three individual choices are stated to be harmful, *all of these* cannot be right either. Only the mono unsaturated fats survive.
